notes: Original lectures (batch 2 of 3). Each lecture feeds eight types: RL, SST, LMCMA, LFIB, HCS, LMCSA, SMW and HIW. Lectures 11 to 15 are backup questions.

sources.title: Improving photosynthesis in crops
sources.body: Over the past century, crop yields have risen mainly through better breeding, fertilisers and irrigation. Many plant scientists believe these gains are slowing, so they are looking at a process that has barely changed: photosynthesis itself. Surprisingly, photosynthesis is quite inefficient. Most crops convert only a few percent of the sunlight they receive into stored energy. One reason is that a key enzyme sometimes grabs oxygen instead of carbon dioxide, wasting energy in the process. Another is that leaves are slow to adjust when they move from bright sunlight into shade. In field trials, researchers have modified tobacco and soybean plants so that their leaves adjust more quickly, and yields increased noticeably. The speaker cautions that results in the field vary, and that farmers will only benefit if the modified crops are accepted by regulators and consumers.

sources.title: Working from home and productivity
sources.body: Does working from home make people more or less productive? The evidence is mixed, partly because productivity is hard to measure. In some studies of call centre staff, employees who worked from home completed more calls, took fewer breaks and were less likely to resign. Other research on creative and technical teams has found that remote work can reduce spontaneous conversations, which are an important source of new ideas and of informal learning for junior staff. Commuting time is another factor. Workers who save an hour of travel each day often spend part of that time working, but they also report better wellbeing. Many organisations now use a hybrid model, with some days in the office and some at home. The speaker suggests that the key question is not where people work, but which tasks benefit from being together.

sources.title: Cane toads in Australia
sources.body: In the nineteen thirties, cane toads were brought from the Americas to Queensland to control beetles that were damaging sugar cane crops. The plan failed. The toads did not control the beetles effectively, but they bred rapidly and spread across northern Australia. Cane toads are poisonous at every stage of life, and native predators such as quolls, goannas and some snakes die after trying to eat them. In some areas, populations of these predators fell sharply as the toads arrived. Researchers have tried many control methods, from trapping to encouraging community toad-collecting days, but none has stopped the spread. A more promising idea is taste aversion training. Predators are given small toads or toad sausages that make them sick without killing them, so they learn to avoid toads. The story is often used to show the risks of introducing species.

sources.title: The origins of writing
sources.body: Writing was not invented to record stories or poetry. In Mesopotamia, the earliest known writing developed more than five thousand years ago from a practical need: keeping track of goods. Officials used small clay tokens to represent items such as grain or sheep. Over time, these tokens were replaced by marks pressed into clay tablets, and the marks gradually became more abstract. By combining signs for sounds with signs for words, scribes could eventually record names, laws and, later, literature. Writing seems to have developed independently in at least a few other places, including China and Mesoamerica. In each case, it was closely linked to the needs of complex states, such as taxation, religion and record keeping. For most of history, only a small group of trained specialists could read and write, so writing also concentrated power.

sources.title: The hidden problem of groundwater depletion
sources.body: Groundwater is water stored underground in layers of rock and sediment called aquifers. It supplies drinking water for billions of people and a large share of the water used for irrigation. Because it is out of sight, its decline often goes unnoticed. When water is pumped out faster than rain can refill the aquifer, the water table falls. Farmers must then drill deeper wells, which costs more energy and money. In coastal areas, over-pumping can allow seawater to move into aquifers, making the water too salty to use. In some regions the ground itself sinks as sediments compact. Satellite measurements of small changes in gravity now allow scientists to estimate groundwater loss across large regions. The speaker argues that groundwater should be managed like a bank account, where withdrawals must not exceed deposits over time.

sources.title: Does social media cause polarisation?
sources.body: It is often claimed that social media has made societies more politically divided. The argument is that algorithms show people content they already agree with, creating so-called echo chambers. The evidence is more complicated. Several studies suggest that most users are actually exposed to a range of views, and that many people get political news from television as well. In some countries, polarisation began increasing before social media became popular. However, researchers have found that emotionally charged and angry posts tend to spread further, which may make disagreements seem more extreme than they really are. In experiments where people stopped using a platform for several weeks, some became slightly less polarised, but the effects were small. The speaker concludes that social media is probably one contributing factor rather than the main cause of polarisation.

sources.title: Carbon capture and storage
sources.body: Carbon capture and storage is a set of technologies that aim to stop carbon dioxide from reaching the atmosphere. At a power station or cement factory, the gas is separated from other exhaust gases, compressed, and transported by pipeline to a storage site, usually a porous rock formation deep underground. Supporters argue that it is essential for industries such as cement and steel, where emissions come from chemical processes as well as from burning fuel. Critics point out that the technology is expensive, that many projects have captured far less carbon than promised, and that it could be used to extend the life of fossil fuel plants. A related idea is direct air capture, which removes carbon dioxide already in the air, but it currently requires large amounts of energy. The speaker believes carbon capture should complement, not replace, cutting emissions.

sources.title: Is there a critical period for language learning?
sources.body: Children who move to a new country usually end up speaking its language with a native-like accent, while adults often keep a noticeable accent, even after decades. This observation led to the idea of a critical period, a window in childhood after which full mastery of a language becomes impossible. Research supports part of this idea. Accent and some aspects of grammar do seem easier to master when learning starts early. However, adults often learn faster at first, especially vocabulary and explicit grammar rules, because they have better memory strategies and more knowledge of the world. Motivation, the amount of exposure and the quality of teaching also make a large difference. Many researchers now prefer to talk about a sensitive period, when learning is easier, rather than a strict deadline. The speaker encourages adult learners not to give up.

sources.title: Base isolation and earthquake engineering
sources.body: Traditional earthquake engineering focuses on making buildings strong enough not to collapse. Base isolation takes a different approach: it separates the building from the ground. Flexible bearings, often made of layers of rubber and steel with a lead core, are placed between the foundations and the structure. During an earthquake, the ground moves sharply, but the bearings absorb much of that movement, so the building above shifts slowly and gently. This protects not only the people inside but also expensive equipment and contents. New Zealand engineers were early developers of lead rubber bearings, and the technology is used in buildings such as Te Papa, the national museum in Wellington, and several hospitals. Base isolation adds cost during construction, so it is mainly used for important buildings. The speaker argues that after major earthquakes, the savings in repairs can outweigh this extra cost.

sources.title: Work in the gig economy
sources.body: The gig economy refers to work arranged through digital platforms, where people are paid for individual tasks such as deliveries, rides or small online projects. For workers, the main attraction is flexibility. People can choose when to work, which suits students, parents and those with other jobs. For consumers, platforms offer convenience and often lower prices. However, most platforms classify workers as independent contractors rather than employees. This means they usually do not receive sick leave, holiday pay or a guaranteed minimum income, and they may bear costs such as fuel and vehicle maintenance. Earnings can also be unpredictable, because algorithms decide who receives work. Courts in several countries have recently examined whether some gig workers should be treated as employees. The speaker suggests that a new category of worker may be needed, combining flexibility with basic protections.

sources.title: The evidence for dark matter
sources.body: When astronomers measure how fast stars orbit the centre of their galaxy, they find something puzzling. Stars far from the centre move almost as fast as those close to it. If galaxies contained only the matter we can see, the outer stars should move much more slowly, just as distant planets orbit the Sun more slowly than nearby ones. One explanation is that galaxies are surrounded by large amounts of invisible material, known as dark matter, which adds extra gravity. Other observations point in the same direction, including the way clusters of galaxies bend light from objects behind them. Despite decades of searching, however, no experiment has directly detected a dark matter particle. A minority of physicists therefore argue that our theory of gravity needs changing instead. The speaker notes that both possibilities would transform our understanding of the universe.

sources.title: Shift work and the body clock
sources.body: Almost every cell in the human body follows a daily rhythm, controlled by a master clock in the brain that is set mainly by light. This circadian system tells us when to sleep, and it also regulates hormones, digestion and body temperature. Shift workers, such as nurses, pilots and factory staff, often work when their body clock expects rest. Their sleep during the day tends to be shorter and lighter, and many experience long-term fatigue. Studies have linked years of night work to higher risks of problems such as weight gain and diabetes, although it is difficult to separate the effect of shift work from other lifestyle factors. Employers can reduce the harm by designing rosters that rotate forward, from morning to evening to night shifts, and by providing bright light at work. Workers are advised to keep bedrooms completely dark.

sources.title: The costs and benefits of desalination
sources.body: Desalination turns seawater into fresh water, and it has become an important source of supply for dry regions. Most modern plants use reverse osmosis, pushing seawater at high pressure through membranes that allow water molecules through but block salt. Several Australian cities, including Perth, built large plants after long droughts, and Perth now obtains a significant share of its drinking water this way. The main advantage is reliability, because the supply does not depend on rainfall. The drawbacks are significant, however. Desalination uses a great deal of electricity, which can increase emissions unless the power comes from renewable sources. The plants also produce concentrated salty brine, which must be released carefully to avoid harming marine life. The speaker concludes that desalination works best as an insurance policy, combined with water saving and recycling.

sources.title: Cities of the Industrial Revolution
sources.body: During the Industrial Revolution, which began in Britain in the late eighteenth century, millions of people moved from the countryside into rapidly growing towns. Factories needed large numbers of workers, and wages, although low, were often higher than on farms. The cities were not ready for this growth. Housing was built quickly and cheaply, families often lived in a single room, and there was little clean water or proper drainage. As a result, diseases such as cholera spread easily, and life expectancy in some industrial cities was lower than in rural areas. Gradually, reformers collected evidence linking poor sanitation to illness. Their work led to laws requiring sewers, clean water supplies and minimum housing standards. The speaker points out that many rapidly growing cities today face similar challenges, and that the history offers useful lessons for modern planners.

sources.title: The limits of plastic recycling
sources.body: Many people assume that plastic placed in a recycling bin will be turned into new products. In reality, only a small fraction of the plastic ever produced has been recycled. There are several reasons. Plastics come in many different types, and they must be sorted carefully because mixed plastics are difficult to process. Food residue and labels contaminate the material. Each time plastic is melted and remade, its quality usually declines, so bottles are often turned into lower value products such as fibres rather than new bottles. For years, some wealthy countries also exported large amounts of plastic waste to other nations, where much of it was never recycled. Chemical recycling, which breaks plastics down into basic chemicals, may help in future but is still expensive. The speaker argues that reducing plastic use is more effective than relying on recycling.
